t26bbe995: Although LED lights have made a huge difference compared to old incandescent bulbs, a lot of energy is still consumed by leaving lights on for no reason. In this worksheet you will calculate how much energy and money could be saved by switching technology AND by switching off lights when leaving the room. You will also see what happens when those small per-bulb amounts are multiplied across a whole school.

tc79bbcef: In this worksheet you will combine the energy formula from worksheet 2A with two new ideas: scaling up to a whole school, and understanding that LABOUR is also a real cost.
t297d2a40: SCALING: a single light bulb costs a few cents per evening. But a school has hundreds of light fixtures. When you multiply small costs by hundreds of bulbs and thousands of hours, the totals can become surprisingly large. Always be explicit about the assumptions you make: how many bulbs, how many hours per day, how many days per year.
tf85d85a9: LABOUR COST: changing a light bulb takes time. For a few minutes of human work this is negligible at home, but in a school sports hall with high ceilings the labour cost can be much larger than the cost of the bulb itself. A maintenance worker often costs the school €30-€50 per hour. So a bulb that needs to be replaced 25 times during the lifetime of one LED is not just 25× the bulb cost - it is also 25× the labour.
t78a81b5e: CO₂ EMISSIONS: every kWh you save also avoids some CO₂. The Dutch electricity grid in 2024 had an average emission factor of about 0.27 kg CO₂ per kWh. This is decreasing every year as more renewable energy is added.

t4532e02c: In a real household, lights are not on for a fixed number of hours every day. The kitchen is bright in the morning and evening; the bedroom is used at night; the bathroom briefly several times per day. Electricity prices on a dynamic contract also change every hour - sometimes negative when there is a surplus of solar or wind power. In this worksheet you will build a more realistic model of household lighting cost.
t36ed3a19: *This worksheet assumes you have completed Worksheets 2A and 2B, or are confident with energy calculations, scaling, and the concept of cost = energy × tariff.*
t8de051c1: In a real household, lights are not on for a fixed number of hours every day. The kitchen is bright in the morning and the evening; the bedroom is used at night; the bathroom briefly several times per day. Building a realistic energy model requires HOURLY USAGE PROFILES rather than averages.
t5fa0188d: DYNAMIC TARIFFS: traditional energy contracts charge a flat €/kWh price regardless of when you use electricity. Dynamic contracts (offered in the Netherlands by suppliers such as ANWB Energie, Tibber and EnergyZero) update the tariff every hour based on the wholesale electricity market. Prices are typically lowest at night and during midday solar peaks, and highest in the morning (07-09) and evening (17-21) demand peaks. Sometimes prices even go negative when there is too much wind or solar production.
t94b57e25: BEHAVIOUR vs TECHNOLOGY: there are two fundamentally different ways to reduce energy use - change your behaviour (use less) or change your technology (use more efficiently). They are not always equivalent. A behavioural change requires constant effort and can fail when habits slip. A technological change is permanent but requires upfront investment.
